planting.note: Plant in partial sun in a hole three times the pot width; backfill 1-2 inches above soil level, water in, and mulch.

directions: This 2026 Southern Living Plant Collection introduction is a semidwarf agapanthus bred for sturdy stems and nearly black buds that open into dark purple flowers starting earlier in the season than most Lily of the Nile types. It stays compact at roughly 14-20 inches tall, forms clumping evergreen foliage, and holds up well to heat and drought once it has settled in. Flowers attract birds and butterflies and work well as cut flowers, making the plant a good fit for borders, accent beds, and container plantings in zones 8a-11b. Feed yearly in spring and prune after flowering to keep the clump tidy.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Blackjack Agapanthus plant page

planting.note: Plant 1-2 inches above grade in full sun to part shade; water deeply and mulch 1-2 inches around the base.

directions: Bred at the University of Georgia, this narrow columnar holly is pitched as a sturdier alternative to Sky Pencil holly, holding its upright shape without splaying open as it ages. New leaves emerge with a purplish-red tint before maturing to deep green, giving the plant seasonal color changes on top of its year-round structure. It tops out around 8 feet tall by only 3 feet wide, making it well suited to narrow entryway plantings, walkway hedges, or tight foundation spots. The plant is hardy to roughly -10 to 0 degrees F across zones 6a-9b and needs only occasional shaping to keep its line crisp.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Red Sky Holly plant page

planting.note: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; bloom is heaviest with more direct light.

directions: This new Southern Living selection of African iris stands out from older Dietes bicolor plantings for its striking cream-and-green variegated foliage, paired with the species' familiar summer flush of small yellow flowers. It forms a tough, clumping, upright evergreen mound that tolerates heat, drought, and coastal conditions once established, and needs essentially no pruning to stay tidy. Hardy to about 15-20 degrees F in zones 8b-11b, it works as an accent or border plant, in mass plantings, containers, or poolside beds.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Dietes Milky Way plant page

planting.note: Plant 1-2 inches above soil level in full sun to part shade; mulch 1-2 inches around the base and feed through the growing season.

directions: Charlie Boy is a dwarf cordyline grown for its blade-shaped, burgundy-and-pink variegated leaves, which the breeder notes hold up to wind better than many cordyline selections and retain color through fall and winter. It forms a compact 2-3 foot mound that fits accent spots, mixed borders, containers, and poolside or coastal plantings, and is listed as tolerant of wet sites. Hardy to roughly 10-20 degrees F across USDA zones 8a-10b, it needs no regular pruning and performs as a long-season foliage anchor rather than a flowering feature plant.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Charlie Boy Cordyline plant page

planting.note: Plant 1-2 inches above grade in a hole twice the root ball's width in full sun to part shade; mulch 1-2 inches, keeping it off the stem.

directions: Lucky Charm is a slow-growing littleleaf boxwood with a naturally compact, rounded shape and small, dark green, elongated leaves that need little corrective shearing. It was selected for strong cold hardiness, down to about -20 to -10 degrees F, and for resistance to boxwood blight and leafminer, two problems that plague older boxwood cultivars. Staying around 2.5-3 feet tall and wide and tolerating shade well, it suits borders, edging, low hedges, and mass plantings in zones 5a-9b. Shape it lightly in early spring before new growth emerges and feed through the growing season.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Lucky Charm Boxwood plant page

planting.note: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; avoid sites that stay soggy.

directions: Selected from hundreds of Western red cedar seedlings, Green Valley is a slower-growing, more restrained alternative to the giant 'Green Giant' arborvitae, reaching only about 10-12 feet in its first decade before maturing to a dense 15-20 foot pyramid. It keeps the classic upright arborvitae silhouette and strong disease tolerance in a size that fits more residential hedges and privacy screens without years of heavy pruning to control. Hardy to about -20 to -10 degrees F across zones 5a-9b, it tolerates full sun to partial shade and needs only light tip-shearing after spring growth if a crisper line is wanted.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection (southernlivingplants.com) — Green Valley Arborvitae plant page
